title: Why Trump will lose (again) on the new challenge to his tariffs
gist: Two former USTR general counsels argue the Trump administration's third attempt at a near-universal tariff — a 10 to 12.5 percent Section 301 levy on 60 countries justified by their alleged failure to curb forced-labor imports — is legally doomed at the Court of International Trade, the Federal Circuit, and likely the Supreme Court, because Section 301 is a selective, not blanket, authority and a blanket use would unconstitutionally transfer Congress's tariff power to the president. They flag Section 232 and the never-used Section 338 of the 1930 Smoot-Hawley Act as the administration's likely next legal vehicles, and note refunds will be slow, partial, and captured by importers of record rather than the households that actually bore the cost.

insights.claim: Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 is by its terms a selective authority requiring a country-specific finding after serious investigation, and nothing in its language or legislative history supports en masse use against 60 countries accounting for most of US trade.

insights.so_what: The distinction between selective and blanket delegated authority is the load-bearing test for every remaining tariff vehicle — apply it to score the survival odds of any new tariff announcement.

insights.claim: In 50 years of Section 301 practice, no president or USTR has ever imposed a blanket tariff on countries accounting for nearly all US trade; comprehensive tariff changes have come only through multilateral trade agreements under authority Congress delegated on a bipartisan basis.

insights.claim: Under Loper Bright v. Raimondo courts exercise independent judgment over the bounds of agency authority even where the statute is ambiguous, and the major questions doctrine adds heightened scrutiny where economic and political stakes are large.

insights.so_what: The post-Chevron doctrinal shift that deregulatory investors welcomed now cuts directly against executive tariff power — the same case law is a systematic headwind for any sweeping unilateral trade action.

insights.claim: A 10 to 12 percent tariff applied to the majority of $4.36 trillion of US imports puts hundreds of billions of dollars at stake and reaches household budgets, inflation, interest rates, and allied relations, which is precisely the scale that triggers major-questions scrutiny.

insights.claim: US Customs has refunded $100 million of tariffs illegally collected under the April 2, 2025 emergency tariff and is still reviewing claims for the other 40 percent of what it collected, while refunds for the February 2026 balance-of-payments tariff cannot even begin until appeals conclude.

insights.claim: Only the importer of record can claim a tariff refund, and US trade law gives courts and Customs no mandate to trace how much of the charge was passed downstream to retailers and consumers, leaving supply-chain participants to negotiate any redistribution among themselves.

insights.so_what: Refund windfalls accrue to whoever held the customs entry, not whoever ate the margin — screen for importers of record with pass-through pricing as the asymmetric beneficiaries.
